text: By government decision, legislative amendments will be prepared regarding the recognition of diplomas issued before 2010.

By decision of the Government of Georgia, legislative amendments will be submitted to Parliament, on the basis of which the problems related to the recognition of diplomas issued before 2010 will be resolved for thousands of citizens, – this was stated by the Minister of Education, Science and Youth of Georgia, Givi Mikanadze.
As the minister noted, according to the amendment, 4-year full-time and 5-year part-time studies will be recognized equally.

According to him, the change will affect students who enrolled in the university under an accredited regime and completed their studies under a non-accredited regime, as well as citizens whom educational institutions enrolled in the university before obtaining a license.

“We had this situation: our citizens were taking the same number of subjects in a 4-year program and receiving the same qualification as they did in the 5-year part-time program. Under the legislation in force until now, the 5-year program was equivalent to a master’s degree, while the 4-year program was awarded a bachelor’s degree. Based on the changes, those who complete the 4-year program will receive a diploma equivalent to a master’s degree, which will significantly help citizens find employment in the field they desire.”

Until 2010, before a unified system was established, there was no registry in the education sector that ensured students were informed. There were cases where certain universities that had not been granted accreditation did not tell applicants about this and enrolled them anyway. Later, when they issued diplomas, graduates were already facing problems with the recognition of these documents.

At the same time, some higher education institutions had authorization for a certain period and then had it suspended during the period of study. The students were also not informed about this, and later the people who graduated from these universities had problems.

“The proposed legislative changes will finally put an end to the long and problematic processes our citizens go through to have their diplomas recognized — they go to court, challenge the procedures, which takes time and effort. All of this will be consigned to history once and for all, and the diplomas of thousands of our citizens will be recognized,” said Givi Mikanadze.
